summary:
Project TERRA is an Earth-observation platform for exploring how ecosystems respond to environmental stress and change over time. Users select an area of interest, discover and process supported NASA Earth datasets, and inspect environmental signals together rather than relying on a single vegetation index.

The pipeline integrates MODIS vegetation indices and land-surface temperature, GPM IMERG precipitation, SMAP soil moisture, and NASA POWER meteorological and solar variables. Product-specific quality flags, spatial grids, temporal cadences, and missing observations are handled before analysis.

TERRA calculates seasonal baselines and anomalies, detects disturbance episodes, evaluates resistance, recovery, stability, and sensitivity, and investigates monotonic trends using Mann–Kendall tests and Theil–Sen slope estimates.

Interactive maps, time-series charts, comparisons, and reports make the results easier to explore and reproduce. TERRA is an experimental research and monitoring aid: its indicators support investigation, not definitive ecological diagnosis or causal proof.
details:
1. Problem and Motivation

Environmental systems are continuously exposed to disturbances such as droughts, extreme temperatures, changing precipitation patterns, and soil moisture deficits. Traditional vegetation monitoring often relies on individual indicators, making it difficult to understand the combined response of ecosystems to environmental stress.

TERRA addresses this challenge by combining multiple Earth observation datasets and examining ecosystem dynamics across space and time.

2. How It Works

TERRA is built around an area-of-interest-based analytical workflow.

Users can select a geographic region, explore available environmental datasets, configure an observation period, and investigate the resulting environmental dynamics.

The geospatial processing pipeline supports multiple NASA Earth observation products:

  • MODIS MOD13Q1 — NDVI and EVI vegetation indices.
  • MODIS MOD11A2 — daytime and nighttime land surface temperature.
  • GPM IMERG — precipitation measurements.
  • SMAP SPL3SMP_E — surface soil moisture.
  • NASA POWER — meteorological and solar radiation variables.

The Geospatial Harmonization Service handles dataset discovery, acquisition, decoding, spatial transformation, temporal harmonization, quality assessment, and dataset provenance.

Different spatial resolutions and observation frequencies are respected rather than treated as interchangeable. Missing measurements and invalid observations are not silently interpreted as zero.

3. Scientific Methodology

TERRA's independent Scientific Core implements several complementary analytical methods:

  • Seasonal climatological baselines and environmental anomaly detection.
  • Persistent disturbance episode identification.
  • Mann–Kendall statistical trend analysis.
  • Theil–Sen robust trend slope estimation.
  • Autocorrelation-aware statistical procedures.
  • Cross-variable correlation and regression analysis.
  • Post-disturbance recovery analysis.

Ecosystem resilience is examined through four separate dimensions:

  • Resistance — the magnitude of an ecosystem's response to disturbances.
  • Recovery — the degree and rate of return toward its previous baseline.
  • Stability — the variability of environmental indicators.
  • Sensitivity — the relationship between environmental drivers and ecosystem responses.

Rather than presenting an unvalidated universal resilience score, TERRA keeps these dimensions separate and communicates the limitations and uncertainty of the available evidence.

4. Architecture and Technology

TERRA uses a modular architecture with independently runnable analytical and processing components.

Frontend:
React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, deck.gl, Zustand, TanStack Query, and Apache ECharts.

Backend:
Python, FastAPI, Granian, Pydantic, and SQLAlchemy.

Scientific Computing:
NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Xarray, Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, h5py, netCDF4, and Zarr.

The system includes a Core API, Geospatial Harmonization Service, Scientific Core, asynchronous Workers, and structured/object storage infrastructure.

The frontend provides interactive geospatial exploration, temporal visualization, comparative analysis, and analytical reporting.

5. Innovation and Impact

The key innovation of TERRA is its emphasis on ecosystem response dynamics rather than isolated satellite indicators.

By combining vegetation, temperature, precipitation, and soil moisture information, the platform helps researchers and environmental analysts investigate potential ecosystem vulnerabilities, identify persistent changes, and compare environmental responses between regions.

TERRA is designed to support environmental monitoring, research, and evidence-based investigation. Its outputs are experimental indicators and do not independently establish ecological degradation or causal relationships.

6. Responsible AI Use

AI-assisted development tools were used to support software implementation, debugging, testing, and technical writing. AI-assisted contributions were reviewed and integrated by the development team. Environmental observations are attributed to their original data providers.
